outcomes.text: 4. What does my family teach me?

explainers.title: 1. Who is in my family?
explainers.body:
Look at the people you live with. Who is in your family? Point to each person and say their name. In the big box, draw your family. You can stick in a photo too.

Now count the people in your picture. How many are there? Say the number out loud to your grown-up.

explainers.title: 2. What do I call them?
explainers.body:
We have special names for the people we love. Point to your picture and say each name out loud.

Here is a happy secret: grandmothers have lovely names all over the world! Ayeeyo here, Naani in India, Nonna in Italy, Nenek in Indonesia. Which one do you like to say?
bullets: What do you call your mother? Sana says Hooyo.
What do you call your father? Sana says Aabo.
What do you call your grandmother? Sana says Ayeeyo.
What do you call your grandfather? Sana says Awoowe.

explainers.title: 3. What do we do together?
explainers.body: Families do lots of things together. Listen to each one, and tick the box if your family does it. Then tell your grown-up your favourite.
bullets: ☐ We cook or go to the market.

explainers.title: 4. What does my family teach me?
explainers.body:
Your family has taught you so many things! Listen to each one. Tick it if you can do it, then say who taught you.

Can you do something else that someone taught you? Tell your grown-up, and show them if you can!

explainers.title: 5. I say thank you
explainers.body: When our family helps us, we can say thank you. We can say the kind words, and we can help at home too. In the box, draw one way you help at home.

headers: Draw one way I help at home

explainers.title: 6. Ask an older person
explainers.body:
Older people know so many things! With your grown-up, find an older person in your family, like Ayeeyo or Awoowe. Ask them one of these questions:

Listen carefully. Then draw or tell your grown-up one thing you found out.
bullets: What games did you play when you were little?
Can you tell me about a special day?

explainers.title: Before you go
explainers.body:
You talked and drew so beautifully! Answer these out loud with your grown-up.

Well done! Now turn to the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet to make your very own My Family poster.
bullets: What is one thing your family taught you?
What did you like best today?

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.
notes: read every part aloud. Your child can point, talk, draw, sing, count and tick. There are no marks. Just have fun together.

sections.title: Before you begin
sections.body:
Hello, and welcome to your child's very first Global Perspectives project at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up. In this subject, five- and six-year-olds do not read books or fill in worksheets on their own. They are too young for that, and that is exactly right. Instead, you and your child look at pictures, talk, point, draw, sing, count and play little games together. Underneath all that fun, your child is quietly growing big skills: talking and listening, sharing, finding things out, and thinking about what they liked.

This first project grows those skills through the warmest topic of all: families. Your child already knows so much about families, because they live in one. That makes this the perfect place to begin.

You do not need to be a teacher, and you do not need anything special. You need a warm voice, a little time about twice a week, some paper and crayons, and a willingness to let your child talk and draw and get things a little bit messy. That is how these skills grow.

sections.title: About this project: What can families teach us?
sections.body:
Over this unit, you and your child will explore one big, gentle question: what can families teach us? Along the way your child will say who is in their family, learn the special names we use for family members, talk about the things families do together, notice what their family has taught them, and find out something from an older person, such as a grandmother or grandfather.

Everything builds towards one happy final task: your child will make a My Family poster and tell someone about it. It does not need to be neat or clever. A picture your child is proud to talk about is a complete success.

sections.title: What your child will gently grow
sections.body:
This project grows four Global Perspectives skills. Here they are in plain words, with what to listen for:

You will not test these skills or give any marks. You simply give your child lots of friendly chances to practise them, and you notice out loud when they do them well. A warm 'That was lovely talking, Sana' teaches more than any worksheet ever could.
items: Talking and listening — saying an idea out loud, and really listening to someone else. Listen for: 'I like ...' and 'What about you?'
Finding out — asking, looking and noticing, such as asking a grandparent what they did when they were little.
Sharing and caring — taking turns, helping at home, and being kind, just like families are.
Thinking about our learning — stopping to say what we liked and what we found out. Listen for: 'I liked ...' and 'I found out ...'

sections.title: How this unit works at Ehel Academy
sections.body:
Children of this age cannot learn on their own, so this unit is led by you, the teacher or parent. Ehel Academy's youngest model has three parts that work together:

There is no rush and no timetable. Spread the little lessons across two or three weeks, or longer. If your child wants to draw their family five times, wonderful. Warmth and curiosity are the whole point.
items: You, the grown-up, leading the way. You read everything aloud, run the simple games, and keep it all warm and playful. Each little lesson is short, about 15 to 25 minutes, and you can split it into smaller pieces or stop when your child has had enough.
Teacher sessions about twice a week. In these short live sessions, children sing, look at pictures together, share their family drawings, and hear other children talk about their families too.

A 24-hour AI tutor, always used with a grown-up. The AI tutor can read a little story aloud, ask your child one friendly question, or sing a short family song. At this age the tutor is always used with you sitting right beside your child, never on their own.

sections.title: Meet Sana and her family
sections.body:
So the lessons feel friendly, we follow a little girl called Sana. She goes to Ehel Academy in Hargeisa, and she loves her family very much. Your child can imagine Sana sitting right beside them.

In Sana's home live Sana, her mother (she calls her Hooyo), her father (she calls him Aabo), her big brother Omar, and her baby sister. Her grandmother, Ayeeyo, and grandfather, Awoowe, live close by and visit often. Sana's friends at Ehel Academy have families too, and every family is a little different:

Notice that none of these families is 'the right one'. They are all different, and they are all lovely. This is one of the quiet, important lessons of the whole unit.
items: Leila lives with her mum and her Ayeeyo. The three of them do everything together.
Idris lives with his dad and his uncle, and he has a big, happy dog.
Amal has a very big family with lots of cousins who all live close by.
Yasmin lives with her mum, her dad, and her two brothers.

sections.title: Welcoming every kind of family
sections.body:
This is the most important part of the guide, so please read it gently. Children come from every kind of family, and each child must feel that their family is completely welcome and special. As you teach, keep the door wide open:

You never need to ask a child to explain their family. Simply let each child draw and talk about the people who love and look after them. If a question ever feels tricky for a particular child, skip it warmly and move on. Kindness always comes first.
items: Some children live with a mother and a father. Some live with one grown-up. Some live with a grandmother, an aunt, an uncle, or older cousins. Some are adopted or fostered. All of these are families.
Some families are big, and some are small. Some children have lots of brothers and sisters, and some have none. Every size is a good size.
Families believe different things, too. Some families are Muslim, some are Christian, and some believe other things. We treat every family with the same kindness.
If a child has lost someone they love, be gentle. Let them draw the family they have now, and the people they love, in whatever way feels right to them.

sections.title: How to run the little lessons
sections.body: Each little lesson has the same simple shape: a short Aim (what it is for, just for you), a Talk about part (to get your child talking), and a Do part (the drawing, singing or sorting). Read the Aim to yourself, then enjoy the Talk about and Do parts with your child. Lots of talking is exactly right. Keep everything short and happy.

sections.title: Lesson 1.1 - Who is in my family?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child can say who is in their family, and begins to feel that every family is different and special.

Talk about. Look together at a picture of a family (Sana's family, a family in a book, or a photo of your own). Ask: 'Who can you see? What are they doing?' Then ask: 'Who is in your family? Who lives in your home with you?' Let your child point and name each person.

Do. Help your child draw their family on the Activity Sheet, or stick in a photo. Then count together: how many people are in your family? Say each person's name warmly. Remember, there is no wrong answer. A family can be big or small.

sections.title: Lesson 1.2 - What do I call them?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child learns the special names we use for the people in a family, and hears that families all around the world use different names.

Talk about. Ask: 'What do you call your mother? Your father? Your grandmother?' Many children in our region say Hooyo for mother, Aabo for father, Ayeeyo for grandmother, and Awoowe for grandfather. Share the names your own family uses.

Do. Play a pointing game: point to each person in your child's family drawing and say their name together. Then share this happy fact: grandmothers have lovely names all over the world. Here she is Ayeeyo. In India, some children say Naani. In Italy, they say Nonna. In Indonesia, they say Nenek. Ask your child which name they like best.

sections.title: Lesson 1.3 - What do we do together?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child talks about the things families do together, and sees that families care for, share with and help each other.

Talk about. Ask: 'What do you like doing with your family?' Some ideas to spark it: eating together, playing, telling stories, cooking, going to the market in Hargeisa, praying, visiting Ayeeyo, or singing. Let your child tell you all about it.

Do. On the Activity Sheet, read out some things families do together and let your child tick the ones their family does, then add one of their own. Then talk about caring and helping: 'How does your family help you? How do you help at home?' Even a small child can tidy a toy, carry something light, or say a kind word. Praise every idea.

sections.title: Lesson 1.4 - What does my family teach me?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child notices things they have learned to do, remembers who taught them, and thinks about how to say thank you.

Talk about. Sana learned to wash her hands from her Hooyo, and to count goats from her Awoowe. Ask your child: 'What can you do now that someone taught you? Who showed you how?' Ideas: wash hands, brush teeth, say hello, count, tie a shoe, or fold a mat.

Do. Fill in the tiny picture chart on the Activity Sheet together: tick something your child can do, and say who taught them. Then talk about being grateful. A lovely way to say thank you is to say the words, and to help at home. Play a quick sorting game with Sana's ideas below, choosing which are good ways for a child to say thank you:

Keep it light and warm. The point is simply that kind words and small helping hands are the best thank-you of all.
items: Buy your family a big new car. (A giggle — a small child cannot do this one!)
Say 'thank you' with a big smile. (Yes — lovely!)
Do something helpful at home, like tidying up. (Yes — wonderful!)

sections.title: Lesson 1.5 - What can I find out from older people?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child asks an older family member a simple question or two (a tiny, gentle interview) and learns something from them, such as a game, a song, a story, or a special day.

Talk about. Older people know so many things! Ask: 'What do you think Ayeeyo or Awoowe did when they were little? What games did they play? What songs did they sing?' Help your child think of one or two questions to ask.

Do. With you beside them, let your child ask an older family member one or two questions and listen carefully. Ask them to share one thing: an old game, a song, a story, or how they celebrate a special day. Families celebrate different special days, and that is lovely: some families celebrate Eid, some celebrate Christmas, and some have other special days, like a naming day or a wedding. Bring back one thing your child found out and enjoy it together.

sections.title: Lesson 1.6 - Show what I have learned
sections.body:
Aim. Your child shows what they have learned about their family by making a poster and telling someone about it, and then thinks about what they liked.

Talk about. Ask: 'What did you find out about your family? What did you like best?' Let your child remember the drawings, the names and the stories from the earlier lessons.

Do. Help your child make their My Family poster and tell someone about it. The tiny steps are in the separate Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Finish with the happy-face reflection there. Celebrate warmly, whatever the poster looks like.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: These are the gentle words your child will meet. Say them often and warmly. There is no need to test them.

rows: The people who love you and look after you.
Grown-ups who look after you. Sana says Hooyo and Aabo.
Your parent's mother and father. Sana says Ayeeyo and Awoowe.
Doing something with other people, not on your own.
To give some of what you have to someone else.
To do something kind and useful for someone.
To look after someone because you love them.
To show someone how to do something.
To find out how to do something new.
The kind words we say when someone helps us.

sections.title: What you will need
sections.body: Nothing fancy at all. Gather a few of these before you start:
items: Paper and crayons or coloured pencils.
One big sheet of paper for the My Family poster.
Glue and, if you like, a family photo or two to stick on.
A few old magazines or pictures to look at and cut out (optional).
The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet from this unit.
A warm voice and a little time, about twice a week.

sections.title: Using the AI tutor together
sections.body:
At this age, the AI tutor is a helper you use side by side with your child, never a babysitter. Sit together, and let the tutor do the things a patient, friendly helper does well:

Whenever you see an Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up) box in your child's sheets, that is your cue to open the tutor together. Keep it short and cheerful, and always stay right there. If the tutor ever suggests something you would rather not do, simply skip it. You are always in charge.
items: Read a story aloud. Ask it to read a short, gentle story about a family, slowly.
Ask one simple question. Ask it to ask your child one friendly question, then let your child answer out loud to you.
Sing a short song. Ask it for a little family song or rhyme to sing together.
Name family words. Ask it how to say 'grandmother' in a few languages, and enjoy the sounds together.

sections.title: The final task: a My Family poster
sections.body:
Everything leads gently to this. Your child will make a My Family poster: a picture of the people they love, with one thing their family has taught them, and then they will tell someone about it using a few simple sentence starters that you read aloud. The full, tiny steps are in the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet.

Your job is to gather the paper and crayons, sit alongside, and celebrate. A wobbly, hand-drawn poster that your child is proud to talk about is exactly what success looks like at this age.

sections.title: Thinking about our learning: a simple reflection
sections.body:
To finish, help your child look back and feel good about what they did. Keep it gentle and spoken. The Mini-Project & Reflection sheet has happy faces to point to, stars to colour, and a few warm questions such as:

This looking-back is a real Global Perspectives skill, and it matters as much as the poster. When children hear that their thinking and their family are valued, they learn a lesson that lasts far longer than any fact.
items: Who is in your family?
What is one thing your family taught you?
What did you like best about making your poster?
Who did you talk to about your family?

sections.title: Keeping it warm and fun
sections.body: You now have everything you need. Go at your child's pace, talk far more than you worry, and celebrate every drawing and every idea. If your child finishes this unit feeling that their family is special and that they can talk about the people they love, then this project has done its job beautifully. Have fun, together.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: This is the big one, and it is so much fun! At Ehel Academy, Sana made a poster all about her family, and now it is your turn. With a grown-up, you are going to make a My Family poster and then tell someone all about it. Take your time, and enjoy every part.

steps.title: Draw the people I love
steps.intro:
In the middle of your big paper, draw the people in your family. Draw everyone who lives with you, and anyone else you love, like Ayeeyo or Awoowe. You can draw a pet too, if you have one. Give everyone a big smile!

Take your time. Your family can be big or small. However you draw it, it is just right.

steps.title: Add their names
steps.intro: Point to each person you drew. With your grown-up, say their name out loud. Your grown-up can help you write a name under each person, or you can just point and say them.

steps.title: Add one thing my family taught me
steps.intro: Your family has taught you so much. Choose one thing, and draw it on your poster. It could be washing your hands, counting, saying hello, or helping at home.

headers: Draw one thing my family taught me

steps.title: Make it beautiful
steps.intro: Now decorate your poster! You can add hearts, colours, the sun, or flowers. At the top, your grown-up can help you write the big title: My Family.

steps.title: Show and tell
steps.intro: Your poster is ready! Now show it to someone you love and tell them about it. Your grown-up will read these starts, and you finish them out loud:
items: This is my family. This is ...
My family taught me to ...
I love my family because ...

reflection.prompt: The thing I like best about my family is ...
One thing I want to say thank you for is ...

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.

selfAssessment.statement: I drew the people in my family.
I said their names out loud.
I added one thing my family taught me.
I told someone about my poster.
